t: Bendigeiduran uab Llyr a oed urenhin coronawc ar yr ynys hon, ac ardyrchawc o goron Lundein.
l: Bendigeidfran son of-Llŷr it-was-that was crowned king over this island, and exalted with the crown of-London.
i: Bendigeidfran son of Llŷr was crowned king over this island, and exalted with the crown of London.
n: The Second Branch opens with the tale's ordinary order: subject first, then the particle a, then the verb (a oed 'was') — the 'abnormal sentence', which stresses nothing and is simply how this prose is built. Bendigeiduran is Bendigeid 'blessed' + bran, softened to uran (u = v, modern f): modern Bendigeidfran. uab ← mab 'son', softened after a name; Llyr is modern Llŷr. urenhin ← brenhin 'king', softened as the complement of oed. ar yr ynys hon 'over this island' is Britain. ardyrchawc 'exalted, splendid'. o goron ← coron 'crown', softened after o; Lundein ← Llundein (Llundain), 'London', softened after the feminine noun coron.

t: A frynhawngueith yd oed yn Hardlech yn Ardudwy, yn llys idaw.
l: And one-afternoon he-was at Harlech in Ardudwy, at a court to-him.
i: And one afternoon he was at Harlech in Ardudwy, at a court of his.
n: A frynhawngueith 'and one afternoon': prynhawn 'afternoon' + gweith 'time', with the spirant mutation after a 'and' (p > ph); the scribe writes the ph sound as f (the Red Book has a phrynhawngweith). Compare A threigylgweith 'and once' in the First Branch. yd oed 'he was': the particle yd comes before the verb when something other than the subject opens the sentence. Hardlech is Harlech (hardd 'fair' + llech 'slab of rock'; d = dd); Ardudwy is the cantref it stands in. yn llys idaw 'in a court to him' = at one of his courts; idaw 'to him' is the preposition y conjugated.

t: Ac yn eisted yd oedynt ar garrec Hardlech, uch penn y weilgi, a Manawydan uab Llyr y urawt y gyt ac ef, a deu uroder un uam ac ef, Nissyen ac Efnyssen, a guyrda y am hynny, mal y gwedei ynghylch brenhin.
l: And sitting they-were on the rock of-Harlech, above the head of the sea, and Manawydan son of-Llŷr his brother together with him, and two brothers of-one mother with him, Nisien and Efnysien, and noblemen besides that, as was-fitting around a king.
i: And they were sitting on the rock of Harlech, above the sea, with Manawydan son of Llŷr, his brother, beside him, and two brothers by the same mother as he, Nisien and Efnysien, and noblemen besides, as was fitting about a king.
n: Ac yn eisted yd oedynt 'and sitting they were': the verbal phrase is put first, so the verb takes yd. ar garrec ← carrec 'rock', softened after ar. uch penn y weilgi 'above the head of the sea': gweilgi is a poet's word for the open sea, softened after the feminine article. y urawt ← brawt 'his brother', softened after y 'his'. y gyt ac ef 'together with him'. deu uroder ← broder 'brothers', softened after deu 'two'; un uam ← mam, softened after un: 'of one mother with him' — half-brothers through their mother, as the next sentence explains. Nissyen and Efnyssen (ss for s) are modern Nisien and Efnysien. guyrda 'noblemen' (gwyr 'men' + da 'good'); y am hynny 'besides that'. mal y gwedei 'as was fitting', the imperfect of gweddu. ynghylch 'around' is yn + kylch with the nasal mutation.

t: Y deu uroder un uam ac ef, meibon oedynt y Eurosswyd o'e uam ynteu Penardim, uerch Ueli uab Mynogan.
l: The two brothers of-one mother with him, sons they-were to Euroswydd by his mother his-own, Penardim, daughter of-Beli son of-Mynogan.
i: The two brothers by his mother were sons of Euroswydd, by his own mother Penardim, daughter of Beli son of Mynogan.
n: The topic is set out first (Y deu uroder …) and then the sentence proper: meibon oedynt 'sons they were', predicate before verb. y Eurosswyd 'to Euroswydd' (ss for s, d = dd). o'e uam is o 'of, by' + 'e 'his' + mam, softened after 'e; ynteu after it marks 'his own', Bendigeidfran's mother as against Euroswydd's. Penardim is the name as both manuscripts write it here — the White Book and the Red Book alike; later editors print Penarddun, but this edition keeps Penardim in the English as well. uerch Ueli ← merch Beli: merch is softened after the name before it, and Beli after the feminine merch. Beli son of Mynogan is the legendary ancestor-king of the Britons.

t: A'r neill o'r gueisson hynny, gwas da oed: ef a barei tangneued y rwg y deu lu, ban uydynt lidyawcaf: sef oed hwnnw Nissyen.
l: And the one of those lads, a good lad he-was: he it-was-that would-make peace between the two hosts, when they-would-be angriest: that-is who that-one was, Nisien.
i: One of those young men was a good youth: he would make peace between two hosts when they were at their angriest. That one was Nisien.
n: A'r neill 'and the one (of two)'. gueisson is the plural of gwas 'youth, lad'. gwas da oed: predicate first again. ef a barei ← parei, the imperfect of peri 'cause', softened after a; the imperfect here is habitual, 'he would make'. tangneued 'peace' (modern tangnefedd). y rwg is a spelling of y rwng 'between' (the next sentence has rwng). y deu lu ← llu 'host', softened after deu: 'the two hosts' means any two hosts at odds. ban uydynt 'when they would be': ban 'when', uydynt ← bydynt, the habitual imperfect of bot. lidyawcaf ← llidyawcaf, superlative of llidyawc 'angry', softened as the complement. sef oed hwnnw Nissyen 'that is, that one was Nisien': sef names the answer.

t: Y llall a barei ymlad y rwng y deu uroder, ban uei uwyaf yd ymgerynt.
l: The other it-was-that would-cause fighting between the two brothers, when it-would-be most that they-loved-each-other.
i: The other would set two brothers fighting just when they loved each other best.
n: Y llall 'the other' — the brother not named here is Efnysien. a barei 'would cause', as above, with the verbal noun ymlad 'fighting'. y deu uroder 'the two brothers': as with y deu lu, any two brothers, not a particular pair. ban uei 'when it would be': uei ← bei, the imperfect subjunctive of bot, softened after ban. uwyaf ← mwyaf 'most'. yd ymgerynt 'that they loved one another': the imperfect of ymgaru, the reciprocal prefix ym- + caru 'love', with the a turned to e by the ending.

t: Ac ual yd oedynt yn eisted yuelly, wynt a welynt teir llong ar dec, yn dyuot o deheu Iwerdon, ac yn kyrchu parth ac attunt, a cherdet rugyl ebrwyd ganthunt, y gwynt yn eu hol, ac yn nessau yn ebrwyd attunt.
l: And as they-were sitting thus, they it-was-that saw thirteen ships, coming from the south of-Ireland, and making towards them, and a going easy swift with-them, the wind behind-them, and drawing-near swiftly to-them.
i: And as they sat there so, they saw thirteen ships coming from the south of Ireland and making towards them, running easily and swiftly with the wind behind them, and fast drawing near.
n: yuelly 'thus, so'. wynt a welynt 'they saw': the abnormal sentence with the imperfect of gwelet. teir llong ar dec 'three ships on ten' = thirteen: teir is the feminine of tri, since llong is feminine; dec is deg (-c for -g). deheu Iwerdon 'the south of Ireland'. parth ac attunt 'towards them': attunt is at 'to' conjugated, third person plural. a cherdet ← kerdet 'going', with the spirant mutation after a; rugyl 'easy, free' (rhugl) and ebrwyd 'swift' describe it; ganthunt 'with them' is gan conjugated. yn eu hol 'in their track' = behind them: eu 'their' puts h before the vowel of ol. nessau 'draw near'.

t: “Mi a welaf longeu racco,” heb y brenhin, “ac yn dyuot yn hy parth a'r tir.
l: “I it-is-that see ships yonder,” said the king, “and coming boldly towards the land.
i: “I see ships out there,” said the king, “and they are coming boldly towards the land.
n: Mi a welaf 'I see', the abnormal sentence in speech. longeu ← llongeu 'ships', softened as the object. racco 'yonder, over there'. heb y brenhin 'said the king': heb is the defective verb used only to tag speech. yn hy 'boldly': hy 'bold' with the adverbial yn. parth a'r tir 'towards the land'.

t: Ac erchwch y wyr y llys wiscaw amdanunt, a mynet y edrych pa uedwl yw yr eidunt.”
l: And bid the men of the court to-dress about-them, and to-go to look what intention is theirs.”
i: Bid the men of the court arm themselves, and go and see what they intend.”
n: erchwch is the plural imperative of erchi 'ask, bid'. y wyr ← gwyr 'men', softened after y 'to'. wiscaw amdanunt 'to dress about them' (gwiscaw, softened as the object of the bidding): to put on their gear, which before ships of unknown purpose must mean their arms. amdanunt is am 'about' conjugated, third person plural. y edrych 'to look'. pa uedwl ← medwl 'thought, intention', softened after pa 'what'. yr eidunt 'theirs', the independent possessive.

t: Y gwyr a wiscawd amdanunt ac a nessayssant attunt y wayret.
l: The men it-was-that dressed about-them and that drew-near to-them downward.
i: The men armed themselves and went down towards them.
n: a wiscawd 'dressed' is a third person singular preterite in -awd, the old ending beside -wys: after the relative a the verb may stay singular though the subject is plural. The second verb, a nessayssant 'drew near', is plural (preterite -assant). y wayret 'downwards' (gwaeret 'slope'), down from the rock to the shore.

t: Gwedy guelet y llongeu o agos, diheu oed ganthunt na welsynt eiryoet llongeu gyweirach eu hansawd noc wy.
l: After seeing the ships from near, certain it-was with-them that they-had-not-seen ever ships better-arrayed their appearance than they.
i: When they saw the ships close at hand, they were certain they had never seen ships better fitted out in appearance.
n: Gwedy guelet 'after seeing' (gu = gw). diheu oed ganthunt 'certain it was with them' = they were sure: what one thinks is 'with' one. na welsynt 'that they had not seen': welsynt is the pluperfect (-synt), a tense modern Welsh has lost. gyweirach is the comparative of kyweir 'well-arrayed, in good order', written softened. eu hansawd 'their appearance': h before the vowel after eu (ansawd). noc wy 'than they': no 'than' takes c before a vowel.

t: Arwydon tec, guedus, arwreid o bali oed arnunt.
l: Ensigns fair, seemly, splendid of brocade were on-them.
i: Fair, seemly, splendid ensigns of brocade were on them.
n: arwydon 'signs, ensigns', plural of arwyd. tec 'fair' (teg, -c for -g); guedus 'seemly, fitting'. arwreid, from arwr 'hero', is 'heroic, splendid'; the Red Book has no word here (arwydon tec gwedus o bali). o bali ← pali 'brocade', a rich silk, softened after o. oed 'was', singular after the plural subject that comes first; arnunt 'on them'.

t: Ac ar hynny, nachaf un o'r llongeu yn raculaenu rac y rei ereill, ac y guelynt dyrchauael taryan yn uch no bwrd y llong, a swch y taryan y uynyd yn arwyd tangneued.
l: And at that, behold one of the ships out-going-ahead before the others, and they-saw raising a shield higher than the board of the ship, and the point of the shield upward as a sign of peace.
i: And with that, one of the ships drew out ahead of the others, and they saw a shield raised above the ship's side, its point upward as a sign of peace.
n: Ac ar hynny 'and at that, thereupon'. nachaf 'behold' (like llyma) sets the scene before the eyes, with a verbal noun following. raculaenu is rac 'before' + blaenu 'go first', softened in the compound (b > u): 'outstrip, go out ahead'. Evans prints it spaced, rac ulaenu; it is one compound verb. y rei ereill 'the others'. y guelynt 'they saw', imperfect. dyrchauael 'raising' (dyrchafael). yn uch no 'higher than'. bwrd y llong 'the ship's board', its side. swch 'point', literally a ploughshare; y uynyd 'upward' (mynyd 'mountain', softened). yn arwyd 'as a sign': predicative yn.

t: Ac y nessawys y gwyr attunt, ual yd ymglywynt ymdidan.
l: And the men drew-near to-them, so-that they-could-hear-each-other talk.
i: And the men drew near to them, until each side could hear the other speak.
n: y nessawys 'drew near': verb first, with the particle y; the -wys preterite stays singular before the plural subject y gwyr, who are the king's men gone down to the shore. ual 'so that'. yd ymglywynt 'they could hear one another': the reciprocal ym- + clywet 'hear', imperfect plural. ymdidan 'talk, conversation'.

t: Bwrw badeu allan a wnaethont wynteu, a nessau parth a'r tir, a chyuarch guell y'r brenhin.
l: Putting boats out they-did they-for-their-part, and drawing-near towards the land, and greeting to the king.
i: They for their part put out boats, came in towards the land, and greeted the king.
n: Bwrw badeu allan a wnaethont 'putting boats out they did': a verbal noun, then a, then a form of gwneuthur 'do' — the narrative pattern that means simply 'they put out boats'. wnaethont is a spelling of wnaethant (the Red Book has wnaethant). wynteu 'they for their part' marks the turn to the men in the ships. badeu 'boats', plural of bad. a chyuarch guell 'and greeting': kyuarch gwell, literally 'ask better', with the spirant mutation after a. y'r 'to the'.

t: E brenhin a'e clywei wynteu o'r lle yd oed ar garrec uchel uch eu penn.
l: The king it-was-that heard-them them-for-their-part from the place he-was on a high rock above their head.
i: The king could hear them from where he was, on the high rock above their heads.
n: E brenhin: E is a spelling of the article y. a'e clywei 'heard them': the infixed pronoun 'e 'them' stands between the particle a and the verb; clywei is the imperfect. o'r lle yd oed 'from the place that he was'. garrec ← carrec, softened after ar; uchel 'high'. uch eu penn 'above their head': Welsh keeps the singular for a part each person has one of.

t: “Duw a rodo da ywch,” heb ef, “a grayssaw wrthywch.
l: “God may-he-give good to-you,” said he, “and welcome to-you.
i: “God give you good,” he said, “and welcome to you.
n: Duw a rodo 'may God give': rodo is the present subjunctive of rodi, the mood of wishing, as in Duw a dalo 'may God repay'. ywch 'to you', plural (y conjugated). grayssaw 'welcome' (modern croeso) is the word's own form, not a mutation. wrthywch 'towards you', wrth conjugated: welcome is given 'towards' a person.

t: Pieu yniuer y llongeu hynn, a phwy yssyd pennaf arnunt wy?”
l: Whose is the company of these ships, and who is chiefest over-them they?”
i: Whose is the company in these ships, and who is chief over them?”
n: Pieu 'whose is?' (modern piau). yniuer 'company, host' (niuer with a prefixed y). a phwy 'and who', spirant after a. yssyd 'who is', the relative form of bot. pennaf 'chief', the superlative of penn 'head'. arnunt wy 'over them', ar conjugated with the echoing pronoun.

t: “Arglwyd,” heb wynt, “mae ymma Matholwch brenhin Iwerdon, ac ef bieu y llongeu.”
l: “Lord,” said they, “there-is here Matholwch king of-Ireland, and he owns the ships.”
i: “Lord,” they said, “Matholwch, king of Ireland, is here, and the ships are his.”
n: heb wynt 'said they'. mae ymma 'is here': mae, the 'is' that opens a statement of where something is. ef bieu y llongeu 'he owns the ships': bieu 'owns' always follows its subject, a relic of an old relative construction.

t: “Beth,” heb y brenhin, “a uynnhei ef?
l: “What,” said the king, “would-he-want?
i: “What,” said the king, “does he want?
n: Beth … a uynnhei ef 'what would he want': the question word comes first, then the relative a. uynnhei ← mynnhei, the imperfect of mynnu 'want', softened after a; the scribe writes the n + h of mynnu as nnh. The imperfect is the courteous 'would'.

t: A uyn ef dyuot y'r tir?”
l: Does-he-want to-come to the land?”
i: Does he wish to come ashore?”
n: A uyn ef: A is the question particle, and it softens the verb: uyn ← myn, the present of mynnu. dyuot y'r tir 'to come to the land', to come ashore.

t: “Na uynn, Arglwyd,” heb wynt, “negessawl yw wrthyt ti, onyt y neges a geif.”
l: “He-does-not-want, Lord,” said they, “having-an-errand he-is to-you, unless his errand he-gets.”
i: “He does not, Lord,” they said; “he has come on an errand to you, and not unless his errand is granted.”
n: Na uynn 'wants not': Welsh answers by repeating the verb, here negated with na, which softens it. negessawl 'having an errand' (neges 'errand, business' + the adjective ending -awl). wrthyt ti 'to you', wrth conjugated. onyt 'unless, if not'. y neges a geif 'his errand he gets': the object first, then a; geif ← keif, the present of kaffael 'get', softened after a. The answer joins two thoughts: he will not come ashore, and he will not come unless his errand is granted.

t: “By ryw neges yw yr eidaw ef?” heb y brenhin.
l: “What kind-of errand is his?” said the king.
i: “What manner of errand is his?” said the king.
n: By ryw 'what kind of': by is a spelling of py, pa 'what', and ryw ← rhyw 'kind', softened after it. yr eidaw ef 'his', the independent possessive (eiddo).

t: “Mynnu ymgyuathrachu a thidy, Arglwyd,” heb wynt.
l: “Wanting to-ally-himself-by-marriage with you, Lord,” said they.
i: “He wishes to ally himself with you by marriage, Lord,” they said.
n: Mynnu 'wanting': a verbal noun answers the question, the subject understood. ymgyuathrachu 'to become kin by marriage', from kyuathrach 'kinship by marriage', with the reciprocal ym-. a thidy 'with you': a 'with' and the spirant mutation, t > th; tidy is the doubled, emphatic 'you'.

t: “Y erchi Branwen uerch Lyr y doeth, ac os da genhyt ti, ef a uyn ymrwymaw Ynys y Kedeirn ac Iwerdon y gyt, ual y bydynt gadarnach.”
l: “To ask-for Branwen daughter of-Llŷr he-came, and if good with-you, he it-is-that wants to-bind the Island of the Mighty and Ireland together, so-that they-may-be stronger.”
i: “He has come to ask for Branwen daughter of Llŷr; and if it please you, he wishes to bind the Island of the Mighty and Ireland together, so that both may be the stronger.”
n: Y erchi Branwen … y doeth 'to ask for Branwen he came': the purpose is put first, so the verb takes y. uerch Lyr ← merch Llyr, as uerch Ueli above. os da genhyt ti 'if it is good with you', if you please. ef a uyn 'he wants'. ymrwymaw 'bind together'. Ynys y Kedeirn 'the Island of the Mighty' is Britain: kedeirn is the plural of kadarn 'mighty'. ual y bydynt 'so that they may be'. gadarnach ← kadarnach 'stronger', softened as the complement.

t: “Ie,” heb ynteu, “doet y'r tir, a chynghor a gymerwn ninheu am hynny.”
l: “Yes,” said he-for-his-part, “let-him-come to the land, and counsel we it-is-that will-take we-for-our-part about that.”
i: “Yes,” he said, “let him come ashore, and we shall take counsel about it.”
n: heb ynteu 'said he for his part': ynteu marks the change of speaker. doet 'let him come', the third person imperative of dyuot. a chynghor a gymerwn 'and counsel we will take': here the object stands first, then a; chynghor ← kynghor with the spirant after a, gymerwn ← kymerwn, first person plural present of kymryt, softened after a. ninheu 'we for our part'.

t: Yr atteb hwnnw a aeth ataw ef.
l: That answer it-was-that went to-him.
i: That answer went to him.
n: a aeth 'went', preterite of mynet. ataw 'to him', at conjugated. ef echoes the pronoun.

t: “Minheu a af yn llawen,” heb ef.
l: “I-for-my-part it-is-that go gladly,” said he.
i: “I will go gladly,” he said.
n: Minheu 'I for my part', the conjunctive pronoun, answering the king. a af 'go, will go': af is the first person present of mynet, which serves for the future too. yn llawen 'gladly'.

t: Ef a doeth y'r tir, a llawen uuwyt wrthaw; a dygyuor mawr uu yn y llys y nos honno, y rwng e yniuer ef ac yniuer y llys.
l: He it-was-that came to the land, and glad there-was-being towards-him; and a great mustering was in the court that night, between his company and the company of the court.
i: He came ashore, and was gladly received; and there was a great gathering in the court that night, of his company and the company of the court.
n: Ef a doeth 'he came'. llawen uuwyt wrthaw 'glad there was being towards him' = he was made welcome: uuwyt ← buwyt, the impersonal preterite of bot (the -wyt ending), softened after the adjective that stands first. wrthaw 'towards him'. dygyuor 'muster, gathering'. uu ← bu 'was', softened as after a relative a left unwritten. e yniuer ef 'his company': e for y 'his', and ef echoing it; Evans prints eyniuer as one word.

t: Yn y lle trannoeth, kymryt kynghor.
l: In the place the-next-day, taking counsel.
i: At once, the next day, they took counsel.
n: Yn y lle 'in the place' = at once, straightway. trannoeth 'the next day'. kymryt kynghor 'taking counsel': a verbal noun stands as the whole sentence, with no finite verb at all; the reader supplies 'they'.

t: Sef a gahat yn y kynghor, rodi Branwen y Uatholwch.
l: That-is what was-got in the counsel: giving Branwen to Matholwch.
i: The council resolved to give Branwen to Matholwch.
n: Sef 'that is': it introduces the answer to an implied question — what did they decide? a gahat 'that was got': kahat, the impersonal preterite of kaffael 'get', softened after a; what is 'got' in council is its outcome. rodi 'giving'. y Uatholwch 'to Matholwch', softened after y 'to' (m > u).

t: A honno oed tryded prif rieni yn yr ynys hon; teccaf morwyn yn y byt oed.
l: And she was the-third chief ancestress in this island; the fairest maiden in the world she-was.
i: And she was one of the Three Chief Ancestresses of this island; she was the fairest maiden in the world.
n: honno 'that one', feminine. tryded 'third' is the way the Triads speak: 'the third' of a set of three, so one of three. prif rieni is uncertain: rieni normally means 'parents, ancestors'; some take the word here for rianed 'maidens', which would make her one of the 'three chief maidens'. The Red Book has the same words. The reading 'ancestress' is kept, with that doubt. teccaf morwyn 'fairest maiden': the superlative stands before the noun, and the sentence ends on oed 'she was'.

t: A gwneuthur oed yn Aberfraw y gyscu genti, ac odyno y kychwyn.
l: And making an-appointment at Aberffraw to sleep with-her, and from-there the setting-out.
i: And a time was appointed at Aberffraw for him to sleep with her, and to set out from there.
n: gwneuthur oed 'making an appointment': oed here is not 'was' but the noun oed (oet) 'appointed time, tryst', as in the First Branch's y mae oet y rof i ac ef; the Red Book spells it oet. Aberfraw is Aberffraw in Anglesey, the chief court of Gwynedd (the scribe writes a single f for ff). y gyscu ← kyscu 'sleep', softened after y 'to'. genti 'with her', gan conjugated for a woman. odyno 'from there'. y kychwyn 'the setting out': kychwyn is not softened, so y is the article rather than 'his'.

t: Ac y kychwynassant yr yniueroed hynny parth ac Aberfraw, Matholwch a'y yniueroed yn y llongheu, Bendigeituran a'y niuer ynteu ar tir, yny doethant hyt yn Aberfraw.
l: And set-out those hosts towards Aberffraw, Matholwch and his hosts in the ships, Bendigeidfran and his company for-his-part on land, until they-came as-far-as to Aberffraw.
i: And those companies set out for Aberffraw, Matholwch and his men in the ships and Bendigeidfran and his on land, until they came to Aberffraw.
n: y kychwynassant 'set out': verb first with the particle y, third person plural preterite in -assant. parth ac 'towards' (ac before a vowel). a'y is a 'and' + y 'his'. llongheu 'ships', written with h (as the scribe writes nnh in mynnhei). Bendigeituran: the scribe also writes the name with t. niuer 'company'; ynteu 'he for his part' sets Bendigeidfran against Matholwch. ar tir 'on land': after ar one expects dir, but the phrase is written unsoftened in both manuscripts. yny doethant 'until they came'; hyt yn 'as far as'.

t: Yn Aberfraw dechreu y wled, ac eisted.
l: In Aberffraw beginning the feast, and sitting.
i: At Aberffraw the feast began, and they sat down.
n: Two verbal nouns carry the sentence: dechreu 'beginning', eisted 'sitting'. y wled ← gwled 'feast', softened after the feminine article.

t: Sef ual yd eistedyssant: brenhin Ynys y Kedeirn a Manawydan uab Llyr o'r neill parth idaw, a Matholwch o'r parth arall, a Branwen uerch Lyr gyt ac ynteu.
l: That-is how they-sat: the king of-the-Island of the Mighty and Manawydan son of-Llŷr on the one side to-him, and Matholwch on the other side, and Branwen daughter of-Llŷr together with him-for-his-part.
i: This is how they sat: the king of the Island of the Mighty, with Manawydan son of Llŷr on one side of him and Matholwch on the other, and Branwen daughter of Llŷr beside Matholwch.
n: Sef ual 'that is how'. yd eistedyssant 'they sat', preterite plural in -yssant. o'r neill parth idaw … o'r parth arall 'on the one side of him … on the other side', the phrase the First Branch uses for Pwyll's seating. gyt ac ynteu 'together with him for his part': ynteu points to the last man named, Matholwch, so Branwen sits by her husband-to-be.

t: Nyt ymywn ty yd oydynt, namyn ymywn palleu.
l: Not in a house they-were, but in pavilions.
i: They were not in a house, but in pavilions.
n: Nyt negates the phrase put first: 'not in a house (it was that) they were'. ymywn 'inside' (y mywn). oydynt is a spelling of oedynt 'they were'. namyn 'but, except'. palleu 'pavilions, tents', plural of pall.

t: Ny angassei Uendigeituran eiryoet ymywn ty.
l: Had-not-fitted Bendigeidfran ever inside a house.
i: No house had ever been able to hold Bendigeidfran.
n: Ny angassei 'had not been contained, had not fitted': the pluperfect (-assei) of a verb meaning 'have room, be held' (the Red Book writes eyngassei). Uendigeituran is the subject, softened after the verb, as a subject sometimes is in Middle Welsh. eiryoet 'ever'. The tale says it without comment: Bendigeidfran is a giant.

t: A'r gyuedach a dechreussant.
l: And the carousing it-was-that they-began.
i: And they began the carousing.
n: The object comes first, then a and the verb. gyuedach ← kyuedach 'carousing', the drinking after a meal, softened after the article (it is feminine). dechreussant 'they began', preterite plural of dechreu.

t: Dilit y gyuedach a wnaethant ac ymdidan.
l: Pursuing the carousing they-did, and conversing.
i: They kept up the carousing and the talk.
n: Dilit … a wnaethant 'pursuing they did': dilit (dilyd, -t for -d) 'follow, keep on with', with the gwneuthur pattern. ac ymdidan 'and conversing' follows after the verb.

t: A phan welsant uot yn well udunt kymryt hun no dilyt kyuedach, y gyscu yd aethant.
l: And when they-saw being better for-them to-take sleep than to-pursue carousing, to sleep they-went.
i: And when they saw that it was better for them to sleep than to carry on carousing, they went to bed.
n: pan welsant 'when they saw', preterite. uot ← bot 'being', softened as the object: 'that it was'. udunt 'for them', y conjugated. kymryt hun 'take sleep'. no 'than'. y gyscu yd aethant 'to sleep they went': the purpose first, then yd and the verb.

t: A'r nos honno y kyscwys Matholwch gan Uranwen.
l: And that night slept Matholwch with Branwen.
i: And that night Matholwch slept with Branwen.
n: y kyscwys 'slept', preterite in -wys, verb first after the time phrase. gan Uranwen 'with Branwen', softened after gan (b > u).

t: A thrannoeth, kyuodi a orugant pawb o niuer y llys; a'r swydwyr a dechreusant ymaruar am rannyat y meirych a'r gweisson.
l: And next-day, rising they-did, everyone of the company of-the-court; and the officers it-was-that began to-busy-themselves about the allotting of the horses and the lads.
i: And the next day all the company of the court rose; and the officers set about sharing out lodging for the horses and the grooms.
n: kyuodi a orugant 'rising they did': orugant is the older plural preterite of gwneuthur; the subject pawb o niuer y llys 'everyone of the court's company' follows. swydwyr 'officers' (swydd 'office'). ymaruar is uncertain in sense; both manuscripts have it, and 'busy themselves with, see to' fits the context. rannyat 'sharing out, allotment' (rhannu 'share'), here of quarters. meirych 'horses', plural of march; gweisson 'lads', here the grooms.

t: Ac eu rannu a wnaethant ym pob kyueir hyt y mor.
l: And their sharing they-did into every quarter as-far-as the sea.
i: And they quartered them in every direction as far as the sea.
n: eu rannu 'their sharing' = sharing them: the object of a verbal noun is put as a possessive before it. a wnaethant 'they did'. ym pob kyueir 'in every quarter': yn 'in' becomes ym before p (nasal assimilation); kyueir 'region, direction'. hyt y mor 'as far as the sea'.

t: Ac ar hynny dydgueith, nachaf Efnyssen gwr anagneuedus a dywedassam uchot, yn dywanu y lety meirch Matholwch, a gouyn a wnaeth, pioed y meirch.
l: And at that one-day, behold Efnysien, the un-peaceable man that we-spoke-of above, chancing to the lodging of-the-horses of-Matholwch, and asking he-did whose-were the horses.
i: And one day Efnysien, the quarrelsome man we spoke of above, came upon the stabling of Matholwch's horses, and asked whose horses they were.
n: dydgueith 'one day' (dyd + gweith 'time'). nachaf 'behold' with yn dywanu 'happening, coming by chance'. anagneuedus 'unpeaceable, quarrelsome': an- 'un-' + (t)angneuedus 'peaceable'. a dywedassam uchot 'whom we spoke of above': dywedassam is the first person plural preterite, the storyteller's 'we'; the Red Book adds ni 'we'. y lety ← llety 'lodging', softened after y 'to'. meirch 'horses', the shorter plural beside meirych. a gouyn a wnaeth 'and asking he did'. pioed 'whose was?', the past of pieu.

t: “Meirych Matholwch brenhin Iwerdon yw y rei hyn,” heb wy.
l: “Horses of-Matholwch king of-Ireland are these,” said they.
i: “These are the horses of Matholwch, king of Ireland,” they said.
n: Predicate first: Meirych Matholwch … yw y rei hyn 'the horses of Matholwch are these'. y rei hyn 'these ones'. heb wy, a spelling of heb wynt 'said they'.

t: “Beth a wnant wy yna?” heb ef.
l: “What do they-do they there?” said he.
i: “What are they doing there?” he said.
n: Beth a wnant wy 'what do they do': wnant, the present plural of gwneuthur, softened after a. yna 'there'.

t: “Yma y mae brenhin Iwerdon, ac yr gyscwys gan Uranwen dy chwaer, a'y ueirych yw y rei hynn.”
l: “Here is the king of-Ireland, and he-has-slept with Branwen your sister, and his horses are these.”
i: “The king of Ireland is here, and he has slept with Branwen your sister, and these are his horses.”
n: Yma y mae 'here is': the place first, then y and mae. yr gyscwys 'has slept': yr is the particle ry, which makes a preterite into a perfect and softens the verb (kyscwys > gyscwys). gan Uranwen, as above. dy chwaer 'your sister'. a'y ueirych 'and his horses' (a + y 'his'; meirych softened after y).

t: “Ay yuelly y gwnaethant wy am uorwyn kystal a honno, ac yn chwaer y minheu, y rodi heb uyghanyat i?
l: “Is-it thus they-did they about a maiden as-good as that-one, and a sister to me-for-my-part, her giving without my-permission me?
i: “Is this what they have done with a maiden so fine as she, and my own sister — given her away without my leave?
n: Ay 'is it?' — the question particle a with y, asking about the word that follows: 'is it thus that …?'. am uorwyn ← morwyn 'maiden', softened after am. kystal a honno 'as good as she'. yn chwaer y minheu 'as a sister to me myself': predicative yn, and minheu 'I for my part'. y rodi 'her giving' = giving her away. uyghanyat 'my permission': uy 'my' causes the nasal mutation, k > ngh, written gh here: kanyat (caniatâd).

t: Ny ellynt wy tremic uwy arnaf i,” heb ef.
l: They-could-not they insult greater upon-me,” said he.
i: They could have put no greater insult upon me,” he said.
n: Ny ellynt 'they could not': gallynt, the imperfect plural of gallu, loses its g after ny. tremic 'insult, contempt' (tremyg). uwy ← mwy 'greater', softened. arnaf i 'on me', ar conjugated with the echoing i. The Red Book adds no hwnnw 'than that'.

t: Ac yn hynny guan y dan y meirych, a thorri y guefleu wrth y danned udunt, a'r clusteu wrth y penneu, a'r rawn wrth y keuyn; ac ny caei graf ar yr amranneu, eu llad wrth yr ascwrn.
l: And at-that, thrusting under the horses, and cutting the lips at the teeth on-them, and the ears at the heads, and the tails at the back; and where he-could-not-get grip on the eyelids, cutting-them at the bone.
i: And with that he went in among the horses and cut off their lips at the teeth, their ears at the head and their tails at the rump; and where he could get no grip on the eyelids, he cut them away to the bone.
n: Ac yn hynny 'and at that'. A run of verbal nouns with no finite verb; the reader supplies 'he'. guan y dan y meirych 'thrusting under the horses': gwanu 'stab, thrust'; the sense is that he went at them with a blade, though the exact picture is not clear. a thorri ← torri 'cut', spirant after a. guefleu 'lips'; danned 'teeth'; udunt 'on them', the disadvantaged party. clusteu 'ears'; rawn 'tail-hair' (rhawn, r for rh); keuyn 'back' (cefn). ny caei 'he could not get': caei is the imperfect of kaffael; after ny one expects chaei, which the Red Book writes. graf ← craf 'grip', softened as object. amranneu 'eyelids'. eu llad 'cutting them': llad is 'strike, cut' as well as 'kill'. ascwrn 'bone'.

t: A gwneuthur anfuryf ar y meirych yuelly, hyt nat oed rym a ellit a'r meirych.
l: And making disfigurement on the horses thus, until there-was-not use that could-be-had with the horses.
i: So he maimed the horses, until there was no use to be made of them.
n: A gwneuthur anfuryf 'and making disfigurement': anfuryf is an- 'un-' + furyf 'form' (ffurf). hyt nat oed 'so that there was not': nat is 'that not'. rym is uncertain; taken as grym 'power, strength', softened, in the sense 'use, good'. a ellit 'that could be': ellit ← gellit, the impersonal imperfect of gallu, softened after a.

t: E chwedyl a doeth at Uatholwch.
l: The tale it-was-that came to Matholwch.
i: The news came to Matholwch.
n: E chwedyl 'the tale, the news' (chwedl): E is the article. at Uatholwch 'to Matholwch', softened after at.

t: Sef ual y doeth: dywedut anfuruaw y ueirych ac eu llygru, hyt nat oed un mwynyant a ellit ohonunt.
l: That-is how it-came: saying the disfiguring of-his horses and their spoiling, until there-was-not one benefit that could-be-had from-them.
i: This is how it came: he was told that his horses had been maimed and spoiled, so that no use at all could be had of them.
n: Sef ual y doeth 'that is how it came'. dywedut 'telling', a verbal noun with the speaker unnamed. anfuruaw 'disfiguring', the verb from anfuryf. y ueirych ← meirych, softened after y 'his'. eu llygru 'their spoiling' = spoiling them. mwynyant 'benefit, use' (mwyniant). ohonunt 'from them', o conjugated.

t: “Ie, Arglwyd,” heb un, “dy waradwydaw yr a wnaethpwyt, a hynny a uynhir y wneuthur a thi.”
l: “Yes, Lord,” said one, “your shaming it-is that has-been-done, and that is-wanted to-do with you.”
i: “Yes, Lord,” said one, “it is an insult to you that has been done, and that is what they mean to do to you.”
n: dy waradwydaw 'your shaming' = shaming you: gwaradwydaw 'disgrace, dishonour', softened after dy, the object put as a possessive. The yr that follows is hard: it may be the particle ry (as in yr gyscwys above) before the relative a, 'that has been done'; the Red Book has heb yr un 'said the one' and no yr here, so the White Book's yr may be that article displaced. a wnaethpwyt 'that was done', the impersonal preterite of gwneuthur (-pwyt). a uynhir 'is wanted': mynhir, the impersonal present of mynnu, softened. y wneuthur 'its doing'. a thi 'with you' (the Red Book: ytti 'to you').

t: “Dioer, eres genhyf, os uy gwaradwydaw a uynhynt, rodi morwyn gystal, kyuurd, gyn anwylet gan y chenedyl, ac a rodyssant ym.”
l: “Assuredly, strange with-me, if my shaming that they-wanted, to-give a maiden so-good, of-equal-rank, so dear to her kindred, as they-gave to-me.”
i: “Indeed, I find it strange that, if they meant to shame me, they should give me a maiden so fine, of a rank so equal to mine, and so dear to her kindred, as the one they gave me.”
n: Dioer 'assuredly', the oath (worn down from Duw a wyr 'God knows'). eres genhyf 'strange with me' = I find it strange. uy gwaradwydaw 'my shaming': after uy 'my' one expects the nasal mutation, ngwaradwydaw, which the scribe does not write here (the Red Book shows it). a uynhynt 'that they wanted', imperfect plural of mynnu. gystal ← kystal 'as good', softened after the feminine morwyn. kyuurd 'of equal rank' (kyf- 'co-' + urdd 'order, rank'). gyn anwylet 'so dear': kyn 'as, so' with the equative of annwyl 'dear'. y chenedyl 'her kindred': y 'her' gives the spirant, k > ch. ac a rodyssant ym 'as they gave to me': ac 'as' after the equatives; ym 'to me'.

t: “Arglwyd,” heb un arall, “ti a wely dangos ef.
l: “Lord,” said another, “you it-is-that see showing it.
i: “Lord,” said another, “you see the proof of it.
n: ti a wely 'you see': wely ← gwely, the second person present of gwelet, softened after a. dangos ef 'showing it', a verbal noun with its object: you see it shown. The Red Book reads dangos mae ef 'showing that it is so'; the White Book has no mae, and nothing is supplied — the words are construed as printed.

t: Ac nyt oes it a wnelych namyn kyrchu dy longeu.”
l: And there-is-not for-you what you-may-do but to-make-for your ships.”
i: And there is nothing left for you to do but make for your ships.”
n: nyt oes 'there is not', the negative of existence. it 'for you', y conjugated. a wnelych 'what you may do', the present subjunctive of gwneuthur, second person. namyn 'but, except'. kyrchu 'make for'. dy longeu ← llongeu, softened after dy.

t: Ac ar hynny arouun y longeu a wnaeth ef.
l: And at that, setting-out to his ships he-did he.
i: And with that he set off for his ships.
n: arouun (modern arofun) 'intend, set out for': a verbal noun with a wnaeth 'he did'. y longeu 'his ships', softened after y 'his', with the sense 'for his ships'.
